Apollonius. An ancient Greek mathematician known as the Great Geometer, living around 262 to 190 BCE. His eight-volume masterwork, the Conics, provided the definitive classical treatment of ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas, and remained the most advanced mathematical treatise of the ancient world through the Renaissance, influencing scientists including Isaac Newton centuries later.

Apollonius advanced far beyond earlier Greek geometry by deriving all conic sections from a single geometric principle: the intersection of a plane with a cone. He proved that an ellipse, parabola, hyperbola, and circle all result from cutting a cone at different angles. This profoundly unifying insight transformed scattered geometric knowledge into a unified theory. He also introduced the terminology now standard in conic sections: focus, directrix, and the eccentricity of a curve, allowing precise algebraic description of these shapes.

Beyond pure mathematics, Apollonius applied conic sections to practical problems in astronomy, particularly planetary orbits, in music and acoustic properties, and in mechanics, demonstrating their real-world utility. His methods anticipated modern analytic geometry by centuries; later mathematicians would use his geometric insights to develop coordinate systems and algebraic representations of curves.

Little is known of his personal life; most biographical details come from references in other ancient texts, reflecting how much ancient knowledge has been lost to time. His work demonstrates the power of unification in mathematics—discovering that seemingly disparate curves are manifestations of a single geometric principle fundamentally changed mathematical thinking. The study of conic sections, revived in Renaissance Europe through Apollonius's texts, became essential to the emerging field of projective geometry and later enabled the development of analytic geometry.
